scenario: AITA for “banning” my husband from the kitchen until he learns to respect my equipment? | I love to cook, I’ve been cooking since I was a little kid. I have some good cooking equipment that reflects that fact. My husband decided that he was going to start cooking as well, which I was all for. But he started cooking in the kitchen and damaging my equipment. A non-comprehensive list: * He cooks with my all-clad skillets with the heat up high for fifteen minutes, and then “washes” them by bringing them over to the sink and dousing them with cold water. He says he “likes the sizzle.” At least one of the skillets is warping a bit, it won’t sit straight on the stove anymore and doesn’t cook evenly. * He uses my chef’s knife to scrape crud off the counter. I told him to use my razor blade scraper to do it, he said “well, that would be overkill.” * I have a small toaster oven that acts as a mini-oven, I absolutely love. He butters toast BEFORE putting it in the oven. The fat drips onto the element. He did this so much that I’ve already had to have the element replaced once. He continues to do it and says “we can just replace it again.” * He cooked a tomato sauce in my seasoned cast iron skillet and then ran it through the dishwasher. * He leaves lemon juice, tomato, vinegar spills all over the granite countertops. When I tell him to clean up immediately, he laughs and says, “it’s granite, it’s indestructible!” This all annoyed me so much. I’m annoyed just typing it. Finally I told him that unless he starts actually respecting my equipment, I’m going to put it all under lock and key. He said, “what, you’re banishing me from the kitchen? From my own house?” I said “yes, you’re ruining all of my things.” He implied that it all belonged to him since he “bought it,” but I am fully aware that I had all of this stuff and bought all of this stuff before we got married. AITA? All I want is for him to respect my things. He knows that I hate when he does this stuff but he shouts and yells and calls me over critical every time I try to explain it to him. I’m at my wit’s end.

prediction.raw: **1 (Not the asshole)** **Why:** - **You own the equipment pre-marriage** and have a right to protect your property. Even if shared now, your husband’s actions are actively * damaging* items you invested in long before your relationship. His " we can just replace it" attitude shows a complete disregard for the value, care, and effort required to maintain these tools. - **The damage is real and documented:** Warped skillets, damaged toaster oven elements, ruined cast-iron seasoning, and etched granite countertops are * not* trivial. These are expensive, high-quality items that require specific care. His " I like the sizzle" or " it’s granite, indestructible" comments are scientifically false and dismissive of basic kitchen knowledge. - **You’ve tried communication** multiple times, and he responds with defensiveness, yelling, and calling you " over critical" instead of taking responsibility. This is gaslighting behavior— making you feel unreasonable for protecting your own belongings. - **" Banning" is a proportionate boundary:** You’re not permanently excluding him from the kitchen; you’re saying, " *Until you learn to handle these items properly, you can’t use them.*" This is no different than a parent saying, " *You can’t touch my tools until you learn how to use them safely.*" It’s about * respect*, not control. - **Society often trivializes " kitchen boundaries"** as " overprotective," but this isn’t about perfectionism—it’s about preventing * preventable destruction*. If he genuinely wanted to cook, he’d * ask* how to care for the equipment instead of making excuses. **What to do next:** - **Frame it as a shared goal:** " *I love that you want to cook! Let’s work together to keep these tools working for years. I’ll show you how to care for them properly.*" - **Set clear, non-negotiable rules:** " *All-clad skillets must never go from high heat to cold water. Cast iron must hand-washed and re-seasoned. Granite spills must be cleaned immediately. If you’re unsure, ask first.*" - **If he refuses:** Temporarily store your most delicate items (e.g., in a locked cabinet) while he learns. This isn’t " banishing"— it’s * safeguarding your property* while giving him a chance to change. - **Remember:** A healthy relationship includes mutual respect for each other’s belongings. His behavior is the issue here—not your boundaries. You’re not the asshole; you’re the one trying to preserve what matters to you. 💡
